blocks.text: Hypokalaemia is defined as a serum potassium concentration below 3.5 mmol/L.

blocks.title: Potassium is the major intracellular cation and plays an essential role in:

blocks.text: Hypokalaemia can cause muscle weakness, paralysis, cardiac arrhythmias and respiratory muscle impairment.
| Severe | Important
Treat urgently when hypokalaemia is associated with significant arrhythmias, paralysis, respiratory muscle weakness or ECG changes, irrespective of the numerical potassium concentration.
Hypokalaemia occurs through three major mechanisms.
**A. Reduced potassium intake**
**B. Increased potassium loss**
**C. Transcellular potassium shift**
Magnesium deficiency frequently accompanies hypokalaemia.
It increases renal potassium loss by impairing normal potassium conservation in the distal nephron.
Consequently, potassium replacement may be ineffective until magnesium deficiency is corrected.
**Clinical pearl:** Always consider checking serum magnesium in moderate, severe or recurrent hypokalaemia.

blocks.title: The objectives of hypokalaemia management are:

items.text: Restore serum potassium to a safe concentration.
Identify and stop ongoing potassium losses.
Avoid excessive potassium replacement and rebound hyperkalaemia.
Initial target: Serum potassium above 3.0 mmol/L in patients with significant hypokalaemia.
General target: Maintain potassium within the laboratory reference range, commonly 3.5–5.0 mmol/L.
Patients with significant cardiac disease or certain arrhythmias may require a higher target, commonly at least 4.0 mmol/L, under appropriate monitoring.

content_groups.group_title: 4.4 IV potassium replacement in severe hypokalaemia

blocks.title: For severe hypokalaemia with ECG changes or life-threatening symptoms:

items.text: Use IV potassium chloride under continuous ECG monitoring.
A rate of 10 mmol/hour is commonly used.
Rates up to 20 mmol/hour may be used in selected critical-care settings through appropriate central venous access and intensive monitoring.

blocks.text: **Clinical pearl:** A potassium infusion rate of 40 mmol/hour is not routine ward treatment. Such exceptionally rapid replacement requires specialist critical-care protocols.

content_groups.group_title: 4.5 Potassium replacement in patients with ongoing losses

blocks.text: Patients with ongoing diarrhoea, vomiting or renal potassium wasting may require additional potassium beyond the initial replacement dose.
Do not simply increase potassium supplementation without reassessing renal function and ongoing losses.
Magnesium deficiency should be corrected alongside potassium replacement.
Hypomagnesaemia increases renal potassium loss and can make hypokalaemia refractory to treatment.
**Adult prescription: Magnesium sulphate**
**Magnesium sulphate 50% injection**

items.text: Duration: Usually over 1 hour, according to severity and local protocol.
Quantity: 4 mL of 50% solution, equivalent to 2 g.

blocks.text: Dilute appropriately before administration. Monitor magnesium, renal function, BP and clinical response.
Further replacement depends on the degree of magnesium deficiency, ongoing losses and renal function.
In severe symptomatic hypomagnesaemia, faster administration may be required under an emergency protocol.

items.text: Reduce or individualise doses in significant renal impairment.
Excessive administration can cause hypotension, bradycardia and respiratory depression.
Monitor deep tendon reflexes in patients receiving substantial magnesium replacement.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. High-yield clinical pearls and examination points

blocks.text: **20 essential facts**

items.text: Hypokalaemia is serum potassium below 3.5 mmol/L.
Severe hypokalaemia is generally below 2.5 mmol/L.
Common causes include vomiting, diarrhoea and diuretic therapy.
Loop and thiazide diuretics increase renal potassium loss.
Potassium chloride is the preferred replacement in most cases.
Oral replacement is preferred when tolerated.
IV potassium is indicated in severe or symptomatic cases.
Never administer concentrated potassium chloride by IV push.
IV potassium must be administered using a controlled infusion pump.
Routine peripheral infusion should generally not exceed 10 mmol/hour.
Higher infusion rates require specialist critical-care monitoring.
Glucose-containing fluids may worsen hypokalaemia through insulin release.
Correct magnesium deficiency alongside potassium deficiency.
Hypokalaemia causes flattened T waves and prominent U waves.
Severe hypokalaemia may cause ventricular arrhythmias.
Hypokalaemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity.
Renal impairment increases the risk of potassium overcorrection.
Check renal function and urine output before IV replacement.
Reassess serum potassium after replacement rather than prescribing repeated doses blindly.
**Y** – Your ECG may show U waves.
**O** – Oral replacement is preferred when possible.
